description: Issue #787's HOST CRASH, executed. A Heritage short alias in REPORTER position whose canonical is a user procedure — `define forward … return 55 … end` then `print fd` — used to escape a raw JavaScript `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'params')` to the embedder, with no `ol-*` diagnostic, no span, and no graceful stop. `spec/error-model.md` admits no such outcome: every failure must surface as a diagnostic a learner can act on, and a studio session would instead have watched the environment fall over. The cause was a two-name disagreement inside one call: `evaluate.ts`'s expression chokepoint resolved `fd` to `forward` for DISPATCH (so `environment.procedures.has("forward")` matched) but handed the UNRESOLVED node on to `callProcedure`, whose `runProcedureBody` re-derives its lookup key from `node.callee.name` — it looked up `fd`, got `undefined`, and dereferenced it. The statement path never had this bug because `canonicalizeHeritageAliasCall` rewrites the callee before dispatching, so the fix makes the expression path rewrite too rather than adding a guard. The conforming outcome is not a diagnostic at all: `fd` IS `forward` (`spec/conformance.md:146`, "alternate spellings only. It does not add new semantics"), so the alias reaches whatever `forward` means — here the learner's own procedure — and prints 55. The event stream proves the canonicalization is total: `procedure-enter`/`procedure-exit` carry `name` `"forward"`, never the surface `fd`, while the `source_span`s still point at the two columns of `fd` the learner actually wrote. Note this reproduces only via `execute()`: `execute()` runs `parse()` only and NEVER `check()`, so no checker fix could have closed it (the same cross-stage split as #741). `"execute": true` for exactly that reason. FORWARD-LOOKING NOTE (ruling #833, slice #839): #833 rules that a built-in name may never be REGISTERED, and every one of the thirteen Heritage alias canonicals — `forward`, `butfirst`, `print`, … — is a built-in name (verified against the registry, not assumed). So once #839 adds the runtime phase-1 guard that enforces it, `define forward` will halt before phase 2 and THIS fixture's setup becomes unreachable by that route. The fix is still correct and still needed: the crash is live today because #839 has not landed and `execute()` enforces nothing itself, and the underlying defect is not about naming rules at all — it is two chokepoints in one call path deriving the callee name differently, which is wrong however the naming rules land. When #839 lands, whoever owns it should re-base this fixture rather than delete it, so the chokepoint agreement stays pinned.
